summary:
Foco Cero is a web application that harmonizes MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) fire hot spots for the Andean Patagonia, calibrated in the Sierras de Córdoba, Argentina. Combining both sensors produces an artificial jump in 2012. More fires are not burning; the instrument’s resolution changed.

We use a nested grid. Each 1 km MODIS cell contains 3×3 VIIRS sub-cells, linked through integer division, so both sensors are compared at the same place and on the same day. Each hot spot receives an attention priority (Low to Extreme) on its own sensor’s scale, based on radiative power density and thermal contrast. The Harmonized series keeps only cells where both sensors agree or differ by one level.

It matters because it gives firefighters and park rangers comparable, verifiable data to prioritize and prevent wildfires.

The app adds terrain slope (SRTM), soil moisture (GLDAS/SMAP), wind (NASA POWER), imagery of historical fires, near-real-time hot spots and International Charter activation criteria, in Spanish and English.

We used Claude (Anthropic) as a development assistant to code the data processing, database and application. The team defined and validated the methodology, and all data come from official sources.
details:
What it does
Foco Cero is a web app that turns two decades of NASA satellite fire detections into consistent, comparable information for wildfire prevention in Andean Patagonia (Comarca Andina and Los Alerces National Park, Argentina). MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) see the same fires at different resolutions: VIIRS records several points where MODIS records one, so merging them creates an artificial jump in 2012.

How it works

  1. Quality and geology filters: low-confidence detections are removed, and cells with persistent heat (volcanoes, industry) are flagged.
  2. Nested grid: every 1 km MODIS cell contains 3×3 VIIRS sub-cells, linked by integer division (quotient = parent cell, remainder = position inside it). Both sensors are compared at the same place and on the same day.
  3. Attention priority per sensor: each detection is ranked Low / Medium / High / Extreme on its own sensor’s scale, using radiative power density (FRP/km²) and thermal contrast (4–11 µm, day and night separately). Saturated VIIRS pixels are handled explicitly.
  4. Harmonized series: only cells seen by both sensors whose priorities agree or differ by one level (4,014 of 4,964 co-detected cells; weighted kappa 0.33). A Combination series weights VIIRS-only cells by a factor α = 0.557, measured in the Sierras de Córdoba (2012–2024).
  5. Context layers: slope (SRTM), soil moisture (GLDAS/SMAP), wind (NASA POWER), NDVI and cloud cover (MODIS), GOES-19 imagery and near-real-time NOAA-20/21 detections.

Benefits and impact
Firefighters, park rangers and civil protection get a fire calendar, risk maps, spread direction, prevention actions and International Charter activation criteria in one place, with every value traceable to its source. The interface is in Spanish and English.

Tools
Python (pandas, NumPy) for the offline ETL; Google Earth Engine; Supabase (PostgreSQL + PostGIS); Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, React-Leaflet and Recharts; deployed on Vercel. Claude (Anthropic) was used as an AI development assistant to write code (ETL, SQL, web app) and translations; the team defined the methodology and reviewed and validated the results.

Creativity
Instead of statistical models, we coordinate both sensors through a simple, exact spatial structure (a nested grid and quotient sets). Agreement between sensors becomes something you can check visually: fill color = MODIS priority, ring color = VIIRS priority.

Considerations
Visual verification of past fires: for 9 key historical fires (including Cholila 2015, Comarca Andina 2021 and the 2025–2026 Patagonian fires), we selected Landsat 8/9, Sentinel-2 and MODIS scenes with Earth Engine. We use band combinations to confirm the detections: shortwave infrared composites (SWIR2–NIR–Red) show the active fire front through smoke, and natural color shows the smoke plume. Each fire also has before / after / recovery images and a burn-severity map (dNBR).
Honest uncertainty: cloud cover, satellite overpass time and sensor saturation are reported, not hidden.
No invented data: if a source fails, the app says so.
Accessibility: colorblind-safe palettes (Viridis).
Transparency: a methodology panel explains every formula and declares AI use.
